chapter: Picnics, wagon advertising and saloon work
title: Ike Jackson offers him a job at McIschus's saloon
summary: While advertising on a wagon he is spotted by bassist Ike Jackson, who offers him a nightly job at a saloon in the district.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Oh, no. Oh, no. So, from Jack Kerris, we were playing once, an advertisement on a Sunday, for a dance over in Gretna, while we'd play mostly every Sunday night, called the Come Clean. We'd make an advertisement on Sunday. On the wagon. On Monday. Yeah, on the wagon. So, I remember one Sunday, on the corner of 8th and Howard, a gentleman called me out the wagon. Which, he lived on 8th Street. It was a row. And he lived in one of the rows. His name was Ike Jackson. Bass violin player. Oh, he played for Tom Anderson for years. So, playing on the corner, like the bands in their play, he called me off the truck and asked who I was, you see. After I explained who I was, why he had played with my uncles. He had visited the house and everything when I was a small boy. Son asked me, how would I like a job in the district? That was on the corner of Murray and Iberville. It was a saloon. Mac Ischus. The proprietor.
What is the last name? Mac?

Yeah, he is the proprietor of it. It used three pieces in there. He had a mandolin player with him. He had a guitar and he was playing bass. And so, he liked my violin playing. And he asked me, would I accept, would like a job, playing every night? So, after he knew my people, I told him, well, it felt good to me. I was still attending school, the Young University, during that time. So, that went up on St. Charles? Well, St. Charles, no, but they sold it. They sold it and renamed it the Gilbert's Academy. And from Gilbert's Academy, it was sold again. That's Leon Teen and Pitt. Leon Teen and St. Charles Avenue.
How old would you have been then?
How old were you then? How old were you?
